region.en: Dry River and Mandeville, Jamaica (symbolic pin: Mandeville)
region.zh: 牙買加乾河與曼德維爾（象徵定位：曼德維爾）

texts.period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921 from named tellers; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories', Memoirs of the American Folk-Lore Society vol. XVII (1924), tale 2 'Tiger as Substitute' (told by William Forbes of Dry River and George Parkes of Mandeville)

summary.en: Anansi tricks a king's two daughters into tying him up over a boiling pot, then swaps the trap for Tiger and escapes; and when caught raiding a field of gub-gub peas he forges a reading from a scrap envelope — 'tie Anansi and let him go when his belly is full' — gets bound instead of caught, then scares the watchman loose by claiming sorcerer's power and finally foists a red-hot iron on Lion by pleading that he never learned to hold a knife and fork.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人以國王之女設局反被困火鍋之上，趁虎經過把刑位換給老虎逃走；又闖入豆田偷豆，偽造信箋教守者『縛蜘蛛、腹飽即放』，屢屢脫身，終以『天生不會持刀叉』的哭訴騙獅子替他綁上火刑位，自己安然遁去。

sensitivity.note: Social amusement tale (Anansi cycle), collected from named Jamaican storytellers; living oral tradition, tales freely shared in public storytelling. Cross-ref: yoruba-ijapa trickster tales (motif family).

passages.text: Anansi courted a king's two daughters and made fools of them, and they caught and bound him and went off to gather wood for a fire under a great kettle of water. While the sisters were gone, Tiger came along. 'Lawd! Brar Tiger, I get into trouble here!' cried Anansi. 'For what?' asked Tiger. 'The king's daughters want to live with me and have tied me here.' Tiger, disgusted, said, 'You fool — untie me and tie me in your place!' Anansi tied Tiger fast and hid himself at a grass-root. When the girls returned and threw down their firewood, the younger cried, 'Sister! the little uncle we tied has turned into a big uncle!' They built the fire, dashed ladles of boiling water over the bound prisoner, and he jumped until the rope popped, tumbling down on the very grass-root where Anansi hid. Anansi laughed, 'Tissin, tissin, tissin!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, Jamaica Anansi Stories, tale 2a 'The King's Two Daughters' (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: A man planted a great field of gub-gub peas and set an illiterate watchman over them; the crop grew lovely and everybody passing admired it. Anansi begged peas and was refused, so he picked up an old envelope, presented it to the watchman, and read it for him: 'The master says — tie Mr. Anansi at the fattest part of the peas, and when his belly is full, let him go.' The watchman did so. Back came the master, furious that no letter had ever been sent; the next day Anansi read the same trick again, but this time the watchman would not free him. Anansi spat threats — 'If you don't let me go, I'll spit on the ground and you'll rot!' — and the frightened watchman untied him, paying Anansi a sorcerer's respect.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 2b 'The Gub-gub Peas' (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the master caught Anansi, carried him to his yard, and bound him beneath a tree, heating a big iron in the fire. As the iron glowed, Lion came by and asked why Anansi was tied. Anansi wept that since the day he was born he had never held a knife and fork, and now the people demanded he should. 'You worthless man!' said Lion. 'I can hold it.' Lion freed him and took his place at the post; when the master came out he found Lion there, drew the red-hot iron from the fire, and shoved it into Lion's ear. Lion plunged, popped the rope, galloped into the bush, and stood panting under the very tree where Anansi watched — who, trembling, shook the leaves until Lion saw him and called him down. Anansi shouted to the household, 'See the man you were looking for!' and Lion galloped away forever, living wild in the bush, while Anansi went free.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 2b, closing episode (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Tiger Made to Prove He Is Anansi's Father's Riding-Horse
title.zh: 老虎被證明是蜘蛛人父親的坐騎

region.en: Dry River, Cock-pit country, Jamaica (symbolic pin: Maroon Town area)
region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地乾河（象徵定位：馬倫鎮一帶）

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 3 'Tiger as Riding-horse' (told by William Forbes, Dry River)

summary.en: When Tiger is courting a fine young miss, Anansi tells the household that Tiger was his father's old riding-horse. Rather than duel the slander, Tiger insists Anansi ride him to the miss's yard as proof — and Anansi builds up saddle, bridle, horsewhip and double spurs step by innocent step, then gallops Tiger through the gate, calling him his father's old horse before the assembled household, and sings 'Poor Tiger dead and gone' as the shamed bully bolts for the woods.
summary.zh: 老虎正追求年輕姑娘，蜘蛛人竟對主人一家說虎是他父親的舊坐騎。老虎為自清，堅持讓蜘蛛人騎到姑娘家門前作證；蜘蛛人卻一步步『天真』地添上鞍、轡、馬鞭與雙刺馬釘，衝門而入高呼『父親的舊馬到了』，眾人嘩然，羞憤的老虎竄入山林，蜘蛛人唱著『可憐的老虎死了』揚長而去。

sensitivity.note: Social amusement tale (Anansi cycle). Note: the story records (and lauds) trickery; the 1924 transcription preserves 1920s vernacular stereotyping of the tellers themselves, avoided here.

passages.text: Tiger, walking to a fine yard to court one of the young misses, heard through the household the word that Anansi had put about: Tiger was Anansi's father's old riding-horse. Furious, Tiger summoned Anansi before the misses to retract it. Anansi sighed that he could not walk at all. 'If I have to carry you on my back, I will carry you,' snapped Tiger. So Anansi fetched a saddle — only to steady his weak feet, he said — a bridle to catch himself when he fell, a horsewhip to fan away flies, and two pairs of spurs, each innocent item explained with a stammer as Tiger, impatient, told him to put the things on and come on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, Jamaica Anansi Stories, tale 3 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Close to the yard Anansi clapped in the spurs, snapped the whip, and made Tiger gallop through the gate before the whole household. 'Carry him into the stable, sah!' Anansi announced. 'I make you to know what Anansi said is true to the fact — you are my father's old riding-horse.' Tiger bolted for the woods in shame while Anansi sang after him, 'Poor Tiger dead and gone!', to the tune the storyteller hummed as Si-lay-na, and the girls were left to decide who, that day, had truly proven anything.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 3, closing (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Tiger Swallows the Family: Anansi in the House-top
title.zh: 虎吞家人：蜘蛛人躲上屋頂

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 5c 'In the House-top' (told by Thomas White, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Sponging off Mr. Goolin day after day, Anansi is set up by Tiger, who lies disguised as a big barrow in the common: Anansi shoulders his prize, brags aloud, and is shaken onto the beard of Tiger beneath. He flees home shouting mis-heard commands — 'shut the back door, open the front door' — and the family takes refuge on the roof, where Anansi saves himself by shoving his hungry children one by one down into Tiger's mouth, then his wife (dangling from his sewn trousers), then tricks the tiger into piling soft trash for his landing and escapes into the rubbish where no one has found him since.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人日日榨取古林先生，老虎化身巨豬伏於公共地設伏；蜘蛛人肩負『戰利品』得意自誇，卻被搖落撞在虎鬚上。他逃回家高喊聽岔的口令，全家躲上屋頂；他為自保把飢餓的孩子一個個推進虎口，又推出吊在褲腳上的妻子；最後哄虎鋪堆軟垃圾作落地之處，趁虎翻尋不見而遁入垃圾堆——至今蜘蛛人仍藏身於碎瓦隙縫之中。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; contains slapstick family-peril comedy, transcribed with the teller's own framing. Paraphrase renders vernacular to standard English.

passages.text: Mr. Goolin had paid Anansi a hundred pounds to make his wife talk, and Anansi lived off the payment, coming to the yard daily for money. When Goolin wearied of him, Tiger offered to stop the nuisance: he turned himself into a big barrow and lay down in the common. Anansi arrived with his rope, 'caught' the barrow, hoisted it across his shoulders, and boasted to himself as he went, 'Ha! if I weren't cunnie, I wouldn't get this big barrow today.' He saw a long beard dropping over his face: it was Tiger, who began to shake him. 'O Brar Tiger, no shake! no shake!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 5c (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Anansi ran for his house, hollering 'Shet de back do', open de front do'!' — which his wife kept mis-hearing as orders to wash the pot and put on dinner. She got all the children up on the roof as Anansi set Tiger down and flew up after them. When each child in turn cried out hungry on the roof, Anansi shoved it down to Tiger, who swallowed it — six children gone, one after another. Anansi slept; his wife, foreseeing her turn, sewed the hem of her frock to the foot of his trousers with needle and thread. When she cried hungry and he shoved her down, her frock-tail caught on his trousers and hauled her back — until she cried hungry again, was shoved again, and Tiger swallowed Mrs. Anansi too.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 5c, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Alone on the house-top, Anansi got hungry himself. 'Brar Tiger,' he called, 'you know what you do? I am a man so fat that if I drop on the bare earth I will mash up — so if you want me to eat me, cut a whole heap of dry trash.' Tiger heaped up the soft rubbish, and Anansi called 'Catch, catch, coming down!' as he let himself fall into it. Tiger searched the trash hard and never found Anansi until today — which is why, the storyteller said, Anansi still lives in the crevices. 'Jack man dora, choose none!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 5c, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 6 'Tiger's Breakfast' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Anansi dines at Tiger's house daily but feeds his host noise-signals that mean 'do not come'. Tiger repays the trick with a real breakfast and a fatal tip: reach into a lying cow for the tripe. Anansi tries it, the frightened cow clamps his arm, bolts downhill dragging him over the stones — and that, the tellers say, is why Anansi's belly is white to this day.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人日日在虎家吃早飯，卻用『有聲來吃、無聲莫來』的信號把老虎支開。老虎識破後以真早飯回敬，並給他一條『妙計』：把手伸入臥牛肚中取內臟。蜘蛛人依計而行，受驚的牛夾緊他的手，狂奔下山拖他跌過碎石——這便是蜘蛛人肚腹至今雪白的緣故。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale (origin of the spider's white belly). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Every day Anansi ate breakfast at Tiger's house, then said, 'Brar Tiger, tomorrow you must come to my house; but when you hear me making noise, come — that time breakfast is on; but if I stay still, you must not come at all.' When Tiger arrived, Anansi's meal was already eaten: 'Brar Tiger, you foot short!' And when Tiger objected that no noise had been made, Anansi said, just so — a man making noise cannot eat. The next day, shamed, he gave Tiger a little breakfast and taught him the table game: when I say 'Nyammy nyammy nyammy', you must say 'Nyam a wha' eat'. Anansi stayed eating everything, and Tiger never got one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, Jamaica Anansi Stories, tale 6 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tiger studied his revenge and served Anansi a generous meaty breakfast, letting the question slip: 'You know how I come by this meat? When I see a cow lie down, I run my hand inside the cow and hold the tripe — so I am never out of meat.' Anansi hurried away and tried it himself. The frightened cow on the hillside turned her head down to the lowland; Anansi cried, 'Do, Brar Cow, don't shut up my hand!' — but the cow clamped the hand the tighter and galloped right down the hill, dragging him over the stones. That, said Richard Morgan of Santa Cruz, is the reason you see Anansi's belly white.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 6, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 7 'Eggs and Scorpions' (told by William Forbes)

summary.en: Anansi and the firefly Blinkie go egg-hunting with a rigged split: Anansi answers the big bird's cry, Blinkie the little bird's — so Anansi carries all the big eggs, and the offended firefly flies off with the light, leaving the spider alone in the dark wood. Hungry Anansi trades phantom eggs for Tiger's sheep-dinner, then steals the sheep itself in the night while Tiger, tipped off by Anansi's feigned crying, is only bitten by the scorpions he had set around his own eggs.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人與螢火蟲進林覓鳥蛋，卻事先安排：大鳥喚時他答『要大蛋』，小鳥喚時讓螢火蟲答——於是大蛋盡歸蜘蛛人。螢火蟲負氣帶走燈光，棄他於黑暗林中。飢餓的蜘蛛人以虛幻之蛋換得虎家的烤羊大餐，夜裡又偷走羊群；老虎反被自己佈下的蠍子螫傷，只聽蜘蛛人假哭家小作掩護。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; Blinkie the firefly is a Jamaican folk figure. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Blinkie and Anansi went into the wood to hunt bird eggs. Anansi made the bargain: when the little bird cries 'Who wants little egg?', Blinkie is to answer; when the big bird cries 'Who wants big egg?', Anansi answers 'Me want big egg!' In the night, with all the big eggs gathered and none for Blinkie, the firefly got vexed, left Anansi in the bush, and flew away with the light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 7 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the dark Anansi came to Tiger's house, where a sheep stood in the yard. 'Brar Tiger, if you give me dinner to eat tonight, I give you all the eggs,' he bargained. Tiger agreed, went to the sheep, and cried, 'Lay out, lay out, sheep!' — and out spread roast fowl, roast duck, and all sorts of things, which Anansi got at. Then he wanted to sleep at Tiger's house; and Tiger, suspicious, set scorpions around the eggs. When Anansi reached in and was bitten, he hollered 'Aye-e-e!' and answered Tiger's question with a tale of crying wife and children — and while Tiger went to bed believing it, Anansi thieved the sheep clean away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 7, closing (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 8 'Tiger's Bone-hole' (told by William Forbes)

summary.en: Tiger boils a great pot of meat and keeps a hole where he throws the bones. Anansi creeps in with wife and three children to eat from the pot; when Tiger comes, the family hides in the bone-hole, and each thrown bone bruises one of them. Anansi keeps his brood hushed until the last bone cracks his own head — then all holler together in the hole, the terrified Tiger bolts from his own house, and the spider family eats his meat and runs him out of it.
summary.zh: 老虎煮好一大鍋肉，另掘『骨洞』丟骨頭。蜘蛛人帶妻小三口潛入鍋邊偷吃；老虎回來，一家五口躲入骨洞，每根擲入的骨頭都砸中一人。蜘蛛人喝令全體噤聲，直到最後一根骨頭砸中自己的頭——於是全家在洞中齊聲大喊，老虎大駭棄屋而逃，蜘蛛人家便吃光他的肉，把他趕出了自家屋子。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale, comic-creepy horror pattern. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Tiger had a big pot of meat, boiled it, left it, and kept a bone-hole where he threw what he finished. Anansi took his wife and three children and said the five of them would go to the house and get into the pot and eat the meat; when they heard Tiger coming, the five of them went into the hole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 8 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tiger came and said, 'Not a creature has eaten this meat but Brar Nansi!' — then began to eat. The first bone he threw into the hole knocked one of the children; as the child started to holler, Anansi said, 'Shut your mouth, sir, don't cry!' Another bone, another child knocked — 'Shut your mouth, sir!' Then the last child, then the mother, each bruised and each hushed, until the final bone knocked Anansi in the head. 'Let us all holler now in the hole!' they cried together — 'Yee! yee-e-e!' — and Tiger, terrified by the chorus in his bone-hole, ran and left his house; Anansi and wife and children came out, took all the meat, and ran him out of his house on account of that bone-hole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 8, closing (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Top Take Off, Catch in the Middle, Lick Clean

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 9 'The Christening' (told by Charles Wright, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Anansi and Tiger find a keg of butter and hide it in the bushes. Week by week Anansi claims a christening letter, returning each time to eat the keg down — the babies, he says, are named 'Top take off', 'Catch in the middle', and 'Lick clean'. At last he leads the exhausted Tiger on a long walk to the hiding place, puts him to sleep, scrapes the keg bare, wipes butter on Tiger's mouth and tail, and shrieks from a tall tree that Tiger has eaten the butter till it melts.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人與老虎尋得一桶牛油藏於叢中。此後每逢一週，蜘蛛人便稱收到受洗請柬外出一次，回來時桶中的牛油已見底——孩子們的名字分別是『削去頂』『抓中間』『舔乾淨』。最後他拖著疲憊的老虎走遍諸地方至藏桶處，哄其入睡，刮盡桶底，在虎嘴虎尾抹上牛油，再爬上高樹大喊：老虎把牛油吃到融化了！

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; frame-story pun on christening names. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi and Tiger both found one keg of butter. Anansi said to Tiger, 'Let us hide it in the bushes.' Some days after, Anansi said he had received a letter for a christening; when he returned, Tiger asked the name of the child. 'The name is Top take off.' Another week, another christening letter — the child's name, Catch in the middle. The last week, another christening — the name, Lick clean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 9 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Anansi said, 'Tiger, let us go look for this keg of butter.' He carried Tiger walking all over the place until he was tired; and when they nearly reached the hiding place, Anansi proposed a sleep. While Tiger slept, Anansi went to the keg, scraped as much butter as he could with a bit of stick, wiped a little on Tiger's mouth and a little at his tail, climbed a tall tree, and made a wonderful alarm that Tiger had eaten the butter until it melted — leaving the thief's accomplice, buttered, to take the blame.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 9, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Eating Tiger's Guts: the Tell-tale Child and the Monkeys' Song
title.zh: 食虎臟：漏嘴的孩子與猴群之歌

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains and Bog, Westmoreland, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山與西摩蘭博格

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 10 'Eating Tiger's Guts' (a, Simeon Falconer; b, Henry Spence)

summary.en: Under the pretence of washing, Anansi trick Tiger into dipping his head in the river, steals his insides, boils them, and lives to hear that Tiger is dead. At his own mock wake he auditions each child's crying — until the youngest, the tell-tale, chanted the truth about 'the guts pupa brought last night', and is locked up. In the second telling Anansi teaches the monkeys to sing 'This time we eat Tiger gut down' as the rightful owner approaches; Tiger, hearing his own fate sung, kills the chorus — and the monkey he catches blames the song on the spider who taught it only yesterday.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人假意『洗頭』騙虎低頭入水，竊其內臟交妻燉煮，次日聞虎已死。他在假喪禮上逐一試聽孩子的哭腔，最小的漏嘴孩子卻唱出『昨夜爸爸拿回的虎臟』真相，被鎖了起來。另一版本：蜘蛛人教猴群見虎便唱『這回我們吃了虎臟』，虎聞歌大怒誅盡猴群，抓到的一隻卻供出——教歌的正是昨日的蜘蛛人。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale (cannibal-comic episode common in the cycle); recorded as folk narrative.

passages.text: Brer Tiger and Brer Anansi went to the river-side, and Anansi said, 'Brer Tiger, take out your inside and wash it out.' Tiger did so. 'Now dip your head in the water and wash it good' — and the moment Tiger's head went under, Anansi took up the inside and ran away with it to his wife Tacoomah to boil. Next morning he heard that Tiger was dead, and he called all the children to rehearse how they would cry at the funeral. Each said, 'Tita Tiger dead!' — but the last child said, 'Same something pupa brought here last night for Ma Tacoomah to boil — Tita Tiger gut.' Anansi locked that tell-tale child up; but the neighbors heard its crying and let it out to the funeral, and when Anansi saw it coming he ran away and took the house-top, and since then he has never come down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 10a 'The Tell-tale' (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In another telling the two were bathing together. Anansi told Tiger, 'Meanwhile bathing, take out your tripe!' — and, coming out first, ate Tiger's tripe, telling him that whoever wanted to know how his tripe went must go down to Monkey town. Anansi got there ahead of him and taught the monkeys a song to sing whenever they saw Tiger coming: 'Dis time, we eat Tiger gut down!' So when Tiger arrived and heard them all singing, he killed off the monkeys — and, catching one, heard it protest that it was Anansi who had come down and taught them the song only yesterday.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 10b 'The Monkeys' Song' (1924); not verbatim.

region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾與乾河

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 11 'Throwing Away Knives' (a, Benjamin Collins; b, William Forbes)

summary.en: A two-act swindle: Anansi loudly throws away a hidden object, goads Tiger into discarding his real knife, then alone can cut the pineapple — 'no man without a knife can eat pine'. In the paired telling he persuades Sheep to leave his spoon behind at the first breakfast-house, then sends him trudging back for it while Anansi eats the meals at every stop.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人高聲丟出暗藏之物，慫恿老虎也真的丟掉刀，隨後獨自持刀吃菠蘿——『沒刀的人吃不了菠蘿』。另一版本中，他哄綿羊在第一家把湯匙留下，再催他回去取匙，自己卻把一路上每頓飯吃光。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale, food-swindle type. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Once Brer Tiger and Brer Anansi were going along. Anansi said, 'Brer Tiger, I am going to throw away my knife, and when you see me throw away mine, you must throw away yours too.' Anansi took something and threw it away; Tiger took his knife and threw it away. When they reached the field to eat pineapple, Brer Nansi had his knife and was eating pine, and Brer Tiger got none. 'Brer Tiger, no man without a knife can eat pine!' said Anansi, cutting himself another slice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 11a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the paired telling, Anansi and Mr. Sheep set out walking over the country, each carrying a spoon. At the first house that gave breakfast, Anansi said, 'Mr. Sheep, leave your spoon here — don't carry it.' At the second he asked where the spoon was; told to fetch it, Sheep trudged back while Anansi ate off the breakfast. At the third, dinner came and went the same way — leave it, go back for it, come back to an empty table — and Mr. Sheep could not get anything to eat that day at all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 11b (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Grace Before Meat: Clap Your Hands and Thank the Lord

region.en: St. Ann's Bay and Bog, Westmoreland, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖安灣與西摩蘭博格

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 12 'Grace Before Meat' (a, Samuel Christie; b, Henry Spence)

summary.en: Traveling with Monkey, Anansi hoards his 'one and a half cunnies' and gets his friend's long tail lowered into a pit to rescue Tiger — climbing a tree while Tiger pounces on the helper. To free Monkey from Tiger's jaws, Anansi coaches the tiger to clap his two hands in joy, crying 'I get Monkey!' — and the primate drops free between the opened arms. In the paired hunting tale, Tiger's catch of a wild goat is lost forever when Anansi teaches him to tuck the goat under his arm and knock hands at the sky, saying 'Thank the Lord!'
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人與猴子同行，自誇『一份半機智』，卻哄猴子的長尾伸入深坑救虎，自己爬上樹看虎撲食恩人。為救猴，他教虎欣喜若狂地擊掌高呼『抓到猴子了』，猴子便從張開的臂間脫身。獵篇裡，老虎捕得山羊，蜘蛛人教他將羊夾在腋下朝天擊掌喊『感謝上主』——山羊一去不回。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; the 'grace before meat' frame satirizes ritual gestures, noted here as folk satire, not religion.

passages.text: Anansi and Monkey were traveling together, two good friends. 'Brer Monkey, how much cunnie do you have?' asked Anansi. 'Plenty, plenty!' said Monkey. Anansi allowed he had only one and a half — he kept the one for himself and gave his friend the half. Travbling on, they saw Tiger in one deep hole. Anansi said, 'You have plenty cunnie and a long tail; send down your tail into the hole and help Brer Tiger!' While Monkey sent down his tail, Anansi climbed a tree. Tiger came out of the hole, laid hold on Monkey — 'I nyam you today!' — and Anansi laughed on the tree while Monkey was in a fix, not knowing how to get away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 12a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the tree Anansi called down to Tiger: 'You have caught Monkey and you are going to eat him? Do like me, now — open your two hands and clap with joy and say, I get Monkey!' The moment Tiger opened his two hands to clap, Monkey got free, and Tiger ran after him while Anansi made his way down from the tree and went home. In the paired tale, Tiger out hunting caught a wild goat where Anansi caught nothing; Anansi taught him that next time he must put the goat under his arm and knock hands at the top, saying 'Thank the Lord!' Tiger did so, the goat got away and was gone — and the two lost their meat that day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tales 12a-b (1924); not verbatim.

region.en: Claremont, St. Ann, and Mandeville, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖安克萊爾蒙特與曼德維爾

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 13 'Day-time Trouble' (a, Susan Watkins; b, Moses Hendricks)

summary.en: Rabbit begs Anansi to be shown 'day-time trouble'. Anansi kills a cub from Tiger's nest, puts the meat in a basket, and has Rabbit hand-deliver it to the tiger father before bolting up a tree: Tiger grabs at Rabbit, who dives into a stone-hole, and when Tiger sends for long-necked Reindeer to dig him out, Anansi slips Rabbit a razor — the decapitated digger terrifies the crowd, and Rabbit learns that day-time trouble, once seen, is never to be asked for again. In the paired telling Rat murders two of four cubs he believes Anansi killed, and carries the dead ones out before Tiger while Anansi's pair come out alive.
summary.zh: 兔子求蜘蛛人讓他見識『白日之禍』。蜘蛛人從虎巢殺死一隻幼虎，把肉裝籃，令兔子親手送到虎父面前便逃；虎撲兔子，兔子鑽入石洞；虎召長頸的馴鹿前來挖掘，蜘蛛人暗塞剃刀——馴鹿落頭而亡，圍觀者四散奔逃。兔子出洞後，蜘蛛人告誡：白日之禍，見過一次，終生莫再求看。另一版：老鼠誤信蜘蛛人所言，殺死四隻虎崽中的兩隻，捧屍迎虎；蜘蛛人的兩隻卻活著出籃。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; the 'day-time trouble' is a Jamaican idiom of dreadful revelation. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Brar Anansi and Brar Rabbit went for a walk, and Rabbit asked Anansi to show him 'day-time trouble'. Going on, Anansi saw Tiger's den with a lot of young Tigers in it, took one out, killed it, and gave Rabbit a basket with a piece of the meat to carry for the Tiger's father, walking him along to Tiger's house and telling Brar Rabbit to hand Tiger the basket. Anansi ran; Tiger caught at Rabbit to kill him, but he got away. Anansi ran up a tree — 'Run, Brar Rabbit, run! run for stone-hole!' — and passed him a razor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 13a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tiger raised a lot of men to get Rabbit out of the hole and sent for Reindeer, who had a long neck to put his head down and dig. But Anansi had told Rabbit that when Reindeer put his head down in the hole, he must take the razor and cut it off. A crowd gathered to see Reindeer take Rabbit out of the hole; instead, the Reindeer's head was taken off, he dropped dead, and the whole crowd ran away with fright. After Rabbit came out, Brar Nansi said to him: 'Brar Rabbit, so day-time trouble stays. So, as long as you live, never ask anybody to show it to you again!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 13a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the paired version, Rat and Anansi came across Tiger's four children. 'Two for me, two for you!' said Anansi, taking up a cub and making the motion of killing it — but putting it alive in his basket. Rat, thinking the cubs dead, killed his own two and carried them in his basket. Meeting Tiger on the home path, Anansi said, 'I saw your babies crying hungry, I took them up to meet you — I carry two, Brer Rat two.' Tiger lay down to nurse them: out of Anansi's basket came one cub alive; out of Rat's, one dead. Tiger sprang at Rat, who ran along the side of a wall until Anansi's cry — 'remember stone-hole!' — saved him, and Tiger, wheeling to revenge himself on Anansi, found the spider under the dry trash where, ever since, Anansi is always found under dry rubbish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 13b 'Rat and Anansi' (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 14 'New Names' (told by Samuel Christie, St. Ann's Bay)

summary.en: Four friends — Anansi, Tiger, Tacoomah, Parrot — bargain that each will take a new name and eat his own mother if she speaks the old one. Anansi engineers the deaths of the other three mothers and then, night after night, drills his own mother in the syllables of 'Che-che-bun-da'. The singing procession arrives; the mothers of his friends are eaten, but Anansi's mother calls out the new name and her life is saved — a bargain Anansi made, the teller says, to feast on the others and save his own.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人、老虎、塔庫馬與鸚鵡四友立約：各取新名，若母親喚出舊名便吃掉母親。蜘蛛人設局令三友之母喪命，又夜夜操練母親記誦『琪琪本達』四字。遊行唱名之夜，三母被食，唯蜘蛛人之母喊出新名保住性命——這正是蜘蛛人與人立約的算計：飽食他人，獨全己母。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale built on a naming taboo (ATU-type name-custom tale); dark comedy, transcribed from named tellers. The covenant-wordplay motif links to Yoruba hidden-name tales (cross_ref: yoruba tradition, motif family only).

passages.text: There were four friends: Anansi, Tiger, Tacoomah and Parrot. Going for a journey, Anansi bargained that the four must change their names, and when they came home each must go to his mother's house — and if his mother called him the old name, he must eat his mother. The new names: Anansi was Che-che-bun-da; Parrot, Green-corn-ero; Tiger, Yellow-prissenda; Tacoomah, Tacoomah-vengeance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 14 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Tacoomah's house Anansi announced the name Tacoomah-vengeance; the mother, not understanding, said, 'Look, my child Tacoomah comes!' — and they killed and ate Tacoomah's mother. At Tiger's mother's, the same; at Parrot's, the same. But every night Anansi cried an excuse and slipped to his own mother's house: 'Mother, if you call me Anansi, they will kill you! You must call me Che-che-bun-da' — repeating it over and over that she might not forget.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 14, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The night came, the party singing along the road: 'Anansi name a Che-che-bun-da, cherry-senda, Yellow-prissenda; Parrot name a Green-corn-ero; Tiger name a Yellow-prissenda; Tacoomah name Tacoomah-vengeance...' As Anansi's mother saw the singers coming, she called, 'Look, my child Che-che-bun-da!' — the new name, and her life was saved. Anansi had made the bargain to feast on the others and save his mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 14, ending (1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 15 'Long-shirt' (told by Moses Hendricks, Mandeville)

summary.en: At a dance in a land where everyone is naked but the one-legged head-man, whose long shirt can talk, Anansi the fiddler plays the crowd to sleep and swaps his old shirt for the magic one — which calls out its own whereabouts. Anansi offloads the enchanted shirt onto Ram-goat in a fresh swap; the head-man's wooden leg stumbles on the goat's single exposed horn, the crowd digs Ram-goat out, drenches him in dirty slops, and leaves him for dead — and the goat, wringing every garment but forgetting his beard, has carried its offensive smell ever since.
summary.zh: 眾人皆裸的國度裡，唯獨裝木腿的頭人穿會說話的長衫。蜘蛛人拉琴使滿場入睡，偷換長衫——衫卻自己喊出下落。蜘蛛人轉手把法衫換給山羊；頭人木腿絆上山羊露出的獨角，群眾掘出山羊，以穢水澆透棄之為屍。山羊擰淨衣物卻忘了擰鬚——山羊一身腥臊之味，便是由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale with etiological ending (goat's smell). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi, Tacoomah and Tiger made a dance — Anansi fiddler, Tacoomah drummer, Tiger tambourine man — and traveled till they came to a country where all the people were naked, except the head-man, who wore a long shirt and had a wooden leg. They invited all the people to the dance; they played until everyone fell asleep, and Anansi stole the head-man's good shirt, putting his own old one on the sleeper. The man woke, missed his shirt — and this shirt could talk. 'Long-shirt, whe' you den?' he called, and the shirt answered, 'Brar Nansi have me on-o!' The chase began; Anansi, frightened, met Brar Ram-goat and swapped: a new shirt for the old. The head-man called; Long-shirt answered, 'Brar Ram-goat have me on now-o!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 15 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ram-goat ran until he was exhausted, dug a hole, and buried himself — leaving one horn outside without knowing it. The head-man's wooden leg could not go fast; he bucked the leg on the projecting horn, fell, and rose thinking it a stump. He cut and cut until he saw blood — 'Look! come now-o, dirtee have blood!' The crowd dug the goat out, took off the long shirt, put on his own old one, and drenched him with all the dirty slops. They left him for dead; then Ram-goat got up, wrung the dirty clothes, wrung every slop from them — but never remembered to wring his beard. Jack man dora! That is the reason the goat has such an offensive smell until this day: he didn't remember to wring his beard!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 15, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Shut Up in the Pot: 'I Got Them Now'
title.zh: 鍋中封人：『這回我可逮住你們了』

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 16 'Shut Up in the Pot' (told by Simeon Falconer, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: In a famine year Anansi weeps to his friends that his family has not eaten bread for days — while his wife's dinner bell rings in the next room. Tiger and Tacoomah, shamed, feed him; Anansi then stages a sorcerer's trick: he enters a boiling pot, is shut in, knocks from within, and emerges alive. Ordered to copy the feat, the two friends are sealed in the pot under a heavy stone while Anansi piles the fire — and as they cook, he tunes up his fiddle: 'I got them now! Them think they got me, but I got them now!'
summary.zh: 饑年之中，蜘蛛人向朋友哭訴家人多日無糧，隔壁卻傳來妻子開飯的呼聲。老虎與塔庫馬羞愧之下拿食物來喂；蜘蛛人隨即上演法術：入沸鍋、加蓋、敲鍋、活著出鍋。兩友奉命效仿，被封入鍋中壓上重石；蜘蛛人加大爐火，一邊聽鍋，一邊調弦唱道：『這回我可逮住你們了！你們以為逮住了我，其實是我逮住了你們！』

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale (boiling-pot duel type); dark comedy from a hard-times frame. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was a very hard time; no food could they get at all, so Anansi's family was well fed in secret. When Brer Tiger and Brer Tacoomah came to see him, he told them that for three or four days his wife and children had not eaten bread. They went home to send him food — and only dodged behind the house to hear his wife call, 'Here! dinner ready!' Back they knocked at the door; the wife opened it, Anansi slunk out of the house, ashamed, and the two friends were given some of the food to eat, and it was all fresh beef.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 16 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: They came back to Anansi, who said, 'I will get the beef, but whatever I tell you to do, you must be sure to do it.' He put a big pot of water on the fire, got into the boiling pot himself, had them shut him up in it, knocked on the pot, and was let out alive. Then he told Brer Tiger he must get in the pot — Tacoomah alongside — shut them up, put a heavy weight on the pot top, went outside, and told his wife to shove up the fire, bigger and bigger. When he came back and found them properly cooked, and they were going to eat now, he was tuning up his fiddle: 'I got them now! I got them now! Them think they got me, but I got them now!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 16, ending (1924); not verbatim.
